1.pericope_label: Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand. And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.

schools.summary: Map the chapter's argument and find the deliberateness of the sin in a gradation of terms, the plan formed at night and executed in the morning.
Take the word for iniquity broadly enough to cover idolatry, uncleanness and oppression, and fasten on the speed with which coveting turns to seizure.
Give the chapter's argument, name the Naboth precedent, and press the legal aggravation that the heritage was not to be sold at all.
Names oppression as the ground of the controversy and sets out its steps, from the desire of what is not one's own to the cursed art of contriving it safely.

debates.question: What marks the sin as deliberate rather than sudden?

positions.position: A gradation in the terms: the plan formed in the night, thought out on the bed, executed in the morning.
The setting of the wits to work with cursed art and policy, so as to accomplish it without exposure or reproach.
The speed of execution: as soon as they covet anything they take it by force, being as bold in executing as skilful in contriving.

outliers.claim: Takes the word for iniquity as broad enough to cover several sins at once, since it is sometimes used for an idol, and so admits idolatry, uncleanness and the coveting of a neighbour's goods together.

Presses the Naboth precedent past the individual case, holding it no isolated incident but an instance of a settled appetite for accumulating land against the law, denounced in the same generation by a contemporary prophet.

themes: Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand.
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.

3.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, against this family do I devise an evil, from which ye shall not remove your necks; neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time is evil. In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people: how hath he removed it from me! turning away he hath divided our fields. Therefore thou shalt have none that shall cast a cord by lot in the congregation of the Lord.

schools.summary: Read the sentence as exact retaliation and construe the disputed clause as a division of the fields to an apostate, meaning an idolatrous king.
Explain that the avaricious were elevated in vain since God waited his time, and show why the loss of the measuring line strikes at the jubilee itself.
Extend the retaliation to the posture of the proud, name the Assyrian instrument, and take the clause of God turning away in displeasure.

positions.position: The enemy, repeating in mockery the lamentations of the sufferers.
A false prophet whose promises came to nothing, or rather a stranger and bystander.
Their friends for them, and they for themselves.
A funeral dirge composed and sung for them as for the dead.

debates.question: How is the clause about dividing the fields to be construed?

positions.position: To an apostate, that is an idolater: the land taken from others is handed to an idolatrous king.
Adverbially of God: turning away from them in displeasure he divided their fields among others.

outliers.claim: Explains why the loss of the measuring line bites, since a line was determined by lot at each jubilee so that every man might regain his own possession, and the threat is that the land should no longer be that people's inheritance.
Presses the loss furthest, that none shall ever return to see the land allotted by line and that they shall no more be the congregation of the Lord, nor their children after them.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, against this family do I devise an evil, from which ye shall not remove your necks; neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time is evil.

In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people: how hath he removed it from me! turning away he hath divided our fields.
Therefore thou shalt have none that shall cast a cord by lot in the congregation of the Lord.

6.pericope_label: Prophesy ye not, say they to them that prophesy: they shall not prophesy to them, that they shall not take shame.

schools.summary: Admit the construction is very confused while the intention is clear, and place the shame on hearers who will not put it away.
Read the prohibition as an attempt to rule God, and report a construction in which the true prophets are silenced while the false are licensed.
Render the verb from the figure of rain and report a rendering that puts the reproach on the prophet himself.
Holds that silencing prophets spits in the face of God's authority and spurns the bowels of his mercy, since sending them is a token of goodwill.

debates.question: Whose shame is meant in the closing clause?

positions.position: The prophet's own: he shall not remove reproaches from himself, since a true prophet is disgraced by the exercise of his office.
The hearers': those who will not take shame to themselves, and to whom the prophesying brings no benefit.

outliers.claim: Reports a construction in which the first word forbids the true prophets while the second permits the false, so that the sentence means let the one speak but not the other.
Finds the arrogance the more remarkable because ungodly men who would take away the liberty of teaching from God's prophets resist them as though they were themselves doubly and trebly prophets.

themes: Prophesy ye not, say they to them that prophesy: they shall not prophesy to them, that they shall not take shame.

7.pericope_label: O thou that art named the house of Jacob, is the spirit of the Lord straitened? are these his doings? do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly? Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war.

schools.summary: Has the prophet expostulating with a people who are the Lord's in name only, and narrows the enmity to the stripping of quiet travellers of cloak and coat.
Read the silencing as an attempt to subject the Spirit to human pleasure, and warn that the concise wording will not yield a single certain sense.
Divide the questions between God and the people, and multiply the fractures of a society at war with itself.

debates.question: Who asks whether the Spirit of the Lord is straitened?

positions.position: The people, continuing their own lamentation, with God answering in the clause that follows.
The prophet, expostulating with a people who bear the name only.
Divided: the first question asserts that God's power is not less than formerly, the second is the people's protest against severe proceedings.

debates.question: Against whom have the people risen as an enemy?

positions.position: Against their brethren of the southern tribes, as in the great slaughter under a king of Israel.
Against one another at every level, tribe against tribe, subjects against kings, the great against the meaner sort.
Against each other generally, robbing and spoiling as well as opposing God.
Against the quiet traveller, stripped of both outer and inner garment.

outliers.claim: Warns that the prophet's words are concise and therefore obscure, so interpreters differ, and works through the disputed opening word before settling for yesterday in the loose Hebrew sense of past time.
Reads the title house of Jacob as a name without the thing, the people being reckoned religious while they are the degenerate offspring of that patriarch.

themes: O thou that art named the house of Jacob, is the spirit of the Lord straitened? are these his doings? do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly?
Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war.

9.pericope_label: The women of my people have ye cast out from their pleasant houses; from their children have ye taken away my glory for ever. Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest: because it is polluted, it shall destroy you, even with a sore destruction. If a man walking in the spirit and falsehood do lie, saying, I will prophesy unto thee of wine and of strong drink; he shall even be the prophet of this people.

schools.summary: State the wrong to widows and orphans as an offence against those under God's tender care, and read the banishment as requital for cruelty to the defenceless.
Explain that the land was God's own rest hidden under his wings, and identify the disease as a wish to be soothed with flatteries.
Press the legal security of the children's estates against sale beyond the jubilee, and apply the false prophet to the hireling of a later age.

debates.question: Whom does the command to arise and depart address?

positions.position: The offenders and the people at large, summoned to prepare for captivity, since men who drove others from their inheritances shall be so driven themselves.
The same, but with a reported alternative that it exhorts the godly to leave a land soon to be destroyed.
Simply the banishment that such conduct must be followed by.

outliers.claim: Explains the weight of calling the land a rest, since it was not merely the people's rest but God's own, hidden under his wings and assigned as an inheritance to a chosen people among whom he dwelt.

Applies the false prophet to his own century, observing how often the worldling who entered the priest's office for a maintenance, and leaves people undisturbed in an unregenerate state, is the better received.

themes: The women of my people have ye cast out from their pleasant houses; from their children have ye taken away my glory for ever.
Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest: because it is polluted, it shall destroy you, even with a sore destruction.
If a man walking in the spirit and falsehood do lie, saying, I will prophesy unto thee of wine and of strong drink; he shall even be the prophet of this people.

12.pericope_label: I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men. The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the Lord on the head of them.

schools.summary: Renders the closing verses without interpretation, the breaker gone up, the gate passed through, the king going before and the Lord at their head.
Divide sharply: one takes the verses for a promise possibly spoken by the false prophet, the other reads them as a commination against the almost universal opinion.
Read the passage as a promise of restoration, explaining the noise of the flock from the clatter of cloven hoofs and the breaker as the giver of deliverance.
States the convention that prophecies end with promises of mercy, fulfilled in part at the return and fully in the kingdom of the Messiah.

debates.question: Are the closing two verses promise or threat?

positions.position: Promise: a restoration fulfilled in part at the return from Babylon and fully in the kingdom of the Messiah.
Threat: a commination denouncing God's future vengeance, though the contrary opinion is almost universally received.
Possibly the false prophet's own words, promising plenty and the return of the captive tribes.

outliers.claim: Turns the images of the passage inside out on his reading, making the broken gate a rout rather than a release, since the ordinary passage would be too narrow for a people going out in confusion, and the king who goes before a king made captive.
Explains the great noise of the assembled flock from the animals themselves, since when a hundred sheep run together the eight hundred divisions of their cloven hoofs make a wonderful clattering.

themes: I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men.
The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the Lord on the head of them.
